Matchup-Driven

There's no bell-cow to bank on — the lead back sees just 48% of carries (league ~59%), a committee that caps any one back's ceiling and makes their rushing props matchup- and script-dependent.

The Offensive Blueprint

When they fall behind they abandon the run entirely — 62% pass while trailing, so their pass-catchers have huge comeback-script ceilings.

By the numbers it's a struggling unit — a 36% success rate (below the 44% average).

The tight end is a genuine centerpiece, not an afterthought — 18% of targets (league ~15%).

In the Red Zone

Inside the 20 they stay aggressive, throwing 56% of the time, which puts scoring equity on the WR1. And with the TE commanding 18% of targets, the tight end is a live red-zone option too.

Defense — The Run Comes Free

They surrender 124 rushing and 209 passing yards per game (league ~120 / ~230). The run moves against them — target opposing RB1s.

They lock down opposing tight ends — just 24 rec yds/game (vs ~35); fade receiving props there.

They lock down backs out of the backfield — just 12 rec yds/game (vs ~18); fade receiving props there.

They leak RB rushing TDs (0.59/game vs ~0.46) — an anytime-TD spot to attack.

A stingy, efficient defense — just 41% success allowed (vs ~44%); temper expectations for opposing skill players.

The Betting Angles

Bottom line: their pass-catchers have massive ceilings in comeback scripts (fade-material as underdogs); opposing RB1s smash on the ground and at the goal line.

Built on 2024–25 data; the profile rebuilds through the season as the current staff and roster set their own tendencies.
